claim.pdf_says: '14.9.39.3   Syntax rules' is printed in exactly the same bold heading style and at the same outline depth as '14.9.39.1   General' and '14.9.39.2   General formats' on page 759 -- all three are fourth-level clause headings subordinate to '14.9.39  SET statement'.
claim.markdown_says: ISO_COBOL.md line 30946: '## 14.9.39.3 Syntax rules' (heading level 2), whereas its siblings are line 30738 '### 14.9.39.1 General' and line 30760 '### 14.9.39.2 General formats' (heading level 3), and their parent is line 30735 '## 14.9.39 SET statement' (heading level 2).
claim.why_it_matters: At level 2 the Syntax rules clause is promoted to a SIBLING of '14.9.39 SET statement' instead of a child of it, so any tool that builds a table of contents, resolves 'see 14.9.39.3', or extracts the rules belonging to the SET statement will detach the syntax rules from their statement. The same defect recurs at line 31157 ('## 14.9.39.4 General rules', page 763) and at lines 31494 / 31570 for 14.9.40.3 / 14.9.40.4, so the repair should be swept -- but only 14.9.39.3 falls on a page in this batch.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED, but the claim mislabels the defect and overstates its consequence, and badly understates its scope. PDF side (rendered E:/Temp/specrecon/v762/spec_p762.png and .../v759/spec_p759.png at 300 dpi, printed folios 732 and 729). Page 762 prints '14.9.39.3 Syntax rules' as a bold clause heading between the Format 17 (message-tag) diagram and the 'FORMAT 1' rule list. Page 759 prints '14.9.39 SET statement', '14.9.39.1 General' and '14.9.39.2 General formats'. Reading the glyphs directly: all four headings are set in the SAME bold face at the SAME point size -- ISO does not vary heading typography between the three-part and four-part clause levels here. So the claim's stated evidence ('printed in exactly the same bold heading style ... as 14.9.39.1 and 14.9.39.2') is literally true but NON-PROBATIVE, because the PARENT 14.9.39 is printed in that identical style too. The dispositive evidence is the clause NUMBER: a four-part number 14.9.39.3 is by ISO's own numbering scheme subordinate to the three-part 14.9.39, exactly as 14.9.39.1 and 14.9.39.2 are. The claim's conclusion is right; its cited reason is not the one that carries it. Markdown side: every line number and every quoted string in the claim verifies verbatim against specs/ISO_COBOL.md -- 30735 '## 14.9.39 SET statement', 30738 '### 14.9.39.1 General', 30760 '### 14.9.39.2 General formats', 30946 '## 14.9.39.3 Syntax rules'. So 14.9.39.3 sits at the same outline depth as its own parent. Refutation attempts, all of which failed: (a) The heading is not absent, reflowed, or on an adjacent line -- number and title are present and character-exact. (b) 'Level 2 for a four-part number' is not a house convention: 620 four-part headings in the file use '###' against 162 using '##', and the immediate neighbours 14.9.35.3/.4, 14.9.36.3/.4, 14.9.41.3/.4 and 14.9.42.3/.4 all use '###' uniformly, so 14.9.39.3 is anomalous against its own local peers. (c) 'First heading on the page gets ##' fails as an explanation -- 14.9.39.1 is '###' and is not first on page 759 only because its parent precedes it there. What the difference actually is: not a MISSING heading but a MIS-LEVELED one. No text is lost; only the markdown outline depth contradicts the PDF's clause numbering. That is still a genuine structural fidelity defect rather than mere formatting, because in markdown the '#' count is the only machine-readable encoding of clause nesting, and here it asserts a parent/child relation that the standard does not have. Two corrections to the claim's impact statement. First, 'resolves see 14.9.39.3' is NOT broken: line 30945 carries '', so anchor-based cross-reference resolution is unaffected. Only TOC depth and 'extract all subclauses of 14.9.39 by heading nesting' are affected. Second, the sweep is far larger than the four sites named. Measured across the whole file: 806 four-part clause headings, of which 162 are at level 2. The cause is a page-slice transcription artifact -- when the parent three-part heading lies on the SAME transcribed page, the child is '###' 551 times vs '##' 12 times; when the parent lies on an EARLIER page, the child is '##' 150 times vs '###' 69 times. The per-page transcriber had no cross-page context and defaulted a page's leading clause heading to '##'. 14.9.39.3 (parent on page 759, child on page 762) is one instance of that systemic pattern, not a one-off.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, but re-scope and re-label it. KIND is not 'missing-heading' -- the heading '14.9.39.3 Syntax rules' is present at specs/ISO_COBOL.md:30946 with its number and title character-exact; it is MIS-LEVELED, emitted as '##' (level 2) where its siblings 14.9.39.1 (:30738) and 14.9.39.2 (:30760) are '###' (level 3), which makes it a sibling of its own parent '## 14.9.39 SET statement' (:30735). The PDF (folio 732) does not distinguish these levels typographically -- 14.9.39, 14.9.39.1, 14.9.39.2 and 14.9.39.3 are all set in the same bold face at the same size -- so the depth is established solely by the four-part clause number, which per ISO numbering makes 14.9.39.3 a child of 14.9.39. IMPACT is narrower than claimed: the anchor '' at :30945 is present and correct, so 'see 14.9.39.3' cross-references still resolve; what breaks is TOC depth and any heading-nesting-based extraction of a statement's subclauses. SCOPE is much wider than the four sites listed: 162 of the file's 806 four-part clause headings are at level 2. It is a page-slice artifact -- when the parent three-part heading is on the same transcribed page the child is '###' (551 vs 12), when the parent is on an earlier page the child is '##' (150 vs 69). Fix it as one document-wide normalization pass that sets heading level from the clause number's component count, not as a per-page repair; 14.9.39.3 is merely the instance that happens to land in this batch.
